topics.title: An Octopus Has Three Hearts
topics.hook: Most animals have one heart. An octopus has three.
topics.keywords: an octopus has three hearts most animals have one heart. an octopus has three. an octopus can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak — the only hard part of its whole body.

topics.title: The Axolotl Can Regrow a Leg
topics.hook: If an axolotl loses a leg, it simply grows a new one.
topics.keywords: the axolotl can regrow a leg if an axolotl loses a leg, it simply grows a new one. a regrown axolotl leg is not a rough copy — it has the correct bones, in the correct order, every time.

topics.title: Bees Dance to Give Directions
topics.hook: A bee that finds flowers comes home and dances the directions.
topics.keywords: bees dance to give directions a bee that finds flowers comes home and dances the directions. bees can also dance about water, tree sap, or a good place to build a new home — not only flowers.

topics.title: The Toughest Animal Is Almost Invisible
topics.hook: The toughest animal on Earth is smaller than the letter O.
topics.keywords: the toughest animal is almost invisible the toughest animal on earth is smaller than the letter o. tardigrades have been on earth for more than 500 million years, long before the first dinosaur and long after the last one.

topics.title: Elephants Listen With Their Feet
topics.hook: Elephants can hear a call from kilometres away — through the ground.
topics.keywords: elephants listen with their feet elephants can hear a call from kilometres away — through the ground. some elephant rumbles travel through the ground for more than ten kilometres — further than they travel through the air.

topics.title: A Chameleon Is Not Hiding
topics.hook: Chameleons mostly change colour to talk, not to hide.
topics.keywords: a chameleon is not hiding chameleons mostly change colour to talk, not to hide. a chameleon's two eyes can look in two different directions at once, then both swing forward to judge distance before the tongue fires.

topics.title: Flamingos Eat Their Colour
topics.hook: A flamingo is born grey. It eats its way to pink.
topics.keywords: flamingos eat their colour a flamingo is born grey. it eats its way to pink. both flamingo parents feed their chick a red liquid made in their own throats, and it drains the colour out of them while they do it.

topics.title: Some Birds Sleep While Flying
topics.hook: A frigatebird can fall asleep in mid-air and keep flying.
topics.keywords: some birds sleep while flying a frigatebird can fall asleep in mid-air and keep flying. frigatebirds have been tracked staying in the air for two months without landing once.

topics.title: Desert Ants Count Their Steps
topics.hook: A desert ant finds its way home by counting how far it walked.
topics.keywords: desert ants count their steps a desert ant finds its way home by counting how far it walked. saharan silver ants forage at midday, when the sand is hot enough to kill their predators, and sprint at nearly a metre a second.

topics.title: How a Cat Twists in Mid-Air
topics.hook: A falling cat turns itself the right way up with nothing to push against.
topics.keywords: how a cat twists in mid-air a falling cat turns itself the right way up with nothing to push against. cats need a little height to complete the turn — they manage it best from about a metre or more.

topics.title: The Fastest Punch in the Sea
topics.hook: A mantis shrimp punches so fast the water itself boils.
topics.keywords: the fastest punch in the sea a mantis shrimp punches so fast the water itself boils. the collapsing bubble reaches temperatures that briefly rival the surface of the sun, in a space smaller than a grain of sand.

topics.title: Bats See With Sound
topics.hook: A bat can catch a moth in complete darkness without ever seeing it.
topics.keywords: bats see with sound a bat can catch a moth in complete darkness without ever seeing it. a bat must shout and listen without deafening itself, so tiny muscles in its ears clamp shut during each call and release in time for the echo.

topics.title: Spider Silk Beats Steel
topics.hook: Weight for weight, spider silk is stronger than steel.
topics.keywords: spider silk beats steel weight for weight, spider silk is stronger than steel. spiders often eat their old web and reuse the protein to spin a fresh one.

topics.title: The Jellyfish That Grows Backwards
topics.hook: One jellyfish can turn itself back into a baby instead of dying.
topics.keywords: the jellyfish that grows backwards one jellyfish can turn itself back into a baby instead of dying. the reset works even on an adult that has already bred — the equivalent of a grown adult turning back into a baby.

topics.title: A Platypus Hunts With Electricity
topics.hook: A platypus closes its eyes, ears and nose to hunt — and still finds its prey.
topics.keywords: a platypus hunts with electricity a platypus closes its eyes, ears and nose to hunt — and still finds its prey. the platypus lays eggs, makes milk without nipples by sweating it through its skin, and the males have venomous spurs on their back legs.

topics.title: The Longest Journey on Earth
topics.hook: One small bird flies from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, every year.
topics.keywords: the longest journey on earth one small bird flies from the arctic to antarctica and back, every year. an arctic tern's lifetime flying distance is roughly the same as flying to the moon and back three times.

topics.title: The Strangest Mammal Underground
topics.hook: One mammal lives like an insect, barely ages, and can survive without oxygen.
topics.keywords: the strangest mammal underground one mammal lives like an insect, barely ages, and can survive without oxygen. a naked mole-rat can live over thirty years, while a mouse of similar size lives about three.

topics.title: Whale Songs Spread Like Pop Songs
topics.hook: Every male humpback in an ocean sings the same song — and it changes every year.
topics.keywords: whale songs spread like pop songs every male humpback in an ocean sings the same song — and it changes every year. low whale calls can travel for hundreds of kilometres through deep water layers that carry sound unusually well.

topics.title: A Colour-Blind Master of Colour
topics.hook: Cuttlefish match colours they cannot see.
topics.keywords: a colour-blind master of colour cuttlefish match colours they cannot see. cuttlefish skin can also change texture, raising bumps and flaps to imitate seaweed or rough rock.

topics.title: The Beetle That Fires Boiling Spray
topics.hook: A bombardier beetle mixes two chemicals and fires boiling liquid at attackers.
topics.keywords: the beetle that fires boiling spray a bombardier beetle mixes two chemicals and fires boiling liquid at attackers. the pulsing fire rate has been measured at around 500 bursts a second — far too fast to see or hear as separate shots.

topics.title: The Fish That Walks on Land
topics.hook: Mudskippers spend most of their time out of the water.
topics.keywords: the fish that walks on land mudskippers spend most of their time out of the water. a male mudskipper courts by leaping into the air and slapping back down on the mud, making a display visible right across the flats.

topics.title: Honey Never Goes Bad
topics.hook: Archaeologists have found honey in ancient tombs that is still edible.
topics.keywords: honey never goes bad archaeologists have found honey in ancient tombs that is still edible. honey has been used on wounds for thousands of years, and some hospitals still use medical-grade honey on stubborn ones today.

topics.title: Crows Remember Your Face
topics.hook: Wrong a crow once and it may recognise you for years — and tell its friends.
topics.keywords: crows remember your face wrong a crow once and it may recognise you for years — and tell its friends. a crow that decides you are friendly may start leaving you small gifts: buttons, beads, bits of shiny glass.

topics.title: Ants Were Farming Before People
topics.hook: Leafcutter ants have been growing their own food for millions of years.
topics.keywords: ants were farming before people leafcutter ants have been growing their own food for millions of years. leafcutter ants are the biggest herbivores in south american rainforests, out-eating every mammal there.

topics.title: Penguins Take Turns Being Cold
topics.hook: In an Antarctic winter, emperor penguins survive by huddling — and by being fair about it.
topics.keywords: penguins take turns being cold in an antarctic winter, emperor penguins survive by huddling — and by being fair about it. emperor penguin fathers lose almost half their body weight during the wait, then feed the chick with a milk-like substance from their throat.

topics.title: Sharks Are Older Than Trees
topics.hook: Sharks were already swimming before the first tree ever grew.
topics.keywords: sharks are older than trees sharks were already swimming before the first tree ever grew. sharks also predate saturn's rings, on current estimates, and the north star — both are younger.

topics.title: Seahorse Fathers Give Birth
topics.hook: In seahorses, it is the male who gets pregnant.
topics.keywords: seahorse fathers give birth in seahorses, it is the male who gets pregnant. many seahorse pairs greet each other every morning with a slow dance, sometimes changing colour while they do it.

topics.title: Some Birds May See the Earth's Magnet
topics.hook: A migrating robin may not feel the Earth's magnetic field. It may look at it.
topics.keywords: some birds may see the earth's magnet a migrating robin may not feel the earth's magnetic field. it may look at it. a young bird making its first migration alone can still find a wintering ground it has never seen.

topics.title: A Creature With No Brain Solves Mazes
topics.hook: Slime mould has no brain, no nerves and no eyes — and it can find the shortest route.
topics.keywords: a creature with no brain solves mazes slime mould has no brain, no nerves and no eyes — and it can find the shortest route. slime moulds can also learn: taught to cross an unpleasant substance, they get braver, and can pass that habit to another blob they merge with.

topics.title: A Fish That Builds a Battery
topics.hook: An electric eel can deliver a jolt of 800 volts — more than a wall socket.
topics.keywords: a fish that builds a battery an electric eel can deliver a jolt of 800 volts — more than a wall socket. volta named his first battery the 'artificial electric organ' — he built it after studying electric fish.

topics.title: A Day on Venus Is Longer Than Its Year
topics.hook: On Venus, one day lasts longer than one whole year.
topics.keywords: a day on venus is longer than its year on venus, one day lasts longer than one whole year. venus is the hottest planet in the solar system, and it is not the closest one to the sun.

topics.title: Lightning Is Hotter Than the Sun
topics.hook: A lightning bolt is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
topics.keywords: lightning is hotter than the sun a lightning bolt is about five times hotter than the surface of the sun. lightning strikes somewhere on earth about 100 times every second.

topics.title: The Moon Is Slowly Leaving Us
topics.hook: The Moon drifts a little further from Earth every year.
topics.keywords: the moon is slowly leaving us the moon drifts a little further from earth every year. days are getting longer too — about 1.7 milliseconds longer every century, as the moon steals a little of earth's spin.

topics.title: Most Volcanoes Are Underwater
topics.hook: Most of Earth's volcanoes are hidden under the sea.
topics.keywords: most volcanoes are underwater most of earth's volcanoes are hidden under the sea. the sea floor is remade constantly — most of it is younger than 200 million years old.

topics.title: Saturn Would Float in Water
topics.hook: Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a bath.
topics.keywords: saturn would float in water saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a bath. saturn's rings are slowly raining down into the planet, and will not last forever.

topics.title: Why the Sky Is Blue
topics.hook: Sunlight looks white, but it is every colour mixed together.
topics.keywords: why the sky is blue sunlight looks white, but it is every colour mixed together. there is no air on the moon to scatter sunlight, so the sky there stays black even at midday.

topics.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
topics.hook: The Moon never changes shape. You just see a different part of it lit.
topics.keywords: why the moon changes shape the moon never changes shape. you just see a different part of it lit. the moon keeps the same face towards us at all times, so nobody on earth saw its far side until a spacecraft photographed it in 1959.

topics.title: A Shooting Star Is a Grain of Sand
topics.hook: That brilliant streak across the sky is usually smaller than a pea.
topics.keywords: a shooting star is a grain of sand that brilliant streak across the sky is usually smaller than a pea. tonnes of this dust arrive every single day, quietly, mostly unnoticed.

topics.title: Why the Sea Is Salty
topics.hook: Rivers are fresh, yet they are what makes the sea salty.
topics.keywords: why the sea is salty rivers are fresh, yet they are what makes the sea salty. the dead sea is so salty that swimmers float without trying, because salt makes water heavier for its volume.

topics.title: Mountains Are Still Growing
topics.hook: Everest is taller this year than it was last year.
topics.keywords: mountains are still growing everest is taller this year than it was last year. marine fossils have been found near the top of everest — that rock was once the floor of a sea.

topics.title: What Is Inside the Earth
topics.hook: Nobody has drilled even a fiftieth of the way to the centre.
topics.keywords: what is inside the earth nobody has drilled even a fiftieth of the way to the centre. the inner core is roughly as hot as the surface of the sun, yet solid, because the pressure is immense.

topics.title: Seasons Are Not About Distance
topics.hook: Earth is closest to the Sun in January — during the northern winter.
topics.keywords: seasons are not about distance earth is closest to the sun in january — during the northern winter. at the poles the tilt is so extreme that the sun does not set for months, then does not rise for months.

topics.title: Rain Needs Something to Start On
topics.hook: Clean air cannot rain. A raindrop needs a speck of dust to form around.
topics.keywords: rain needs something to start on clean air cannot rain. a raindrop needs a speck of dust to form around. raindrops are not tear-shaped. falling drops flatten underneath, more like a tiny hamburger bun.

topics.title: A Storm Older Than Your Country
topics.hook: Jupiter has a storm that has been raging for centuries.
topics.keywords: a storm older than your country jupiter has a storm that has been raging for centuries. the spot's colour changes over the years, from brick red to pale salmon, and nobody knows exactly what chemical gives it the colour.

topics.title: A Place Light Cannot Escape
topics.hook: Throw a ball hard enough and it escapes Earth. Near a black hole, even light cannot.
topics.keywords: a place light cannot escape throw a ball hard enough and it escapes earth. near a black hole, even light cannot. the gas swirling into a black hole can shine brighter than an entire galaxy before it disappears.

topics.title: Space Is Freezing and Burning at Once
topics.hook: In space you could freeze and overheat at the same time.
topics.keywords: space is freezing and burning at once in space you could freeze and overheat at the same time. the empty space between stars is only a few degrees above absolute zero — the coldest temperature possible.

topics.title: The Next Star Is Terribly Far
topics.hook: The nearest star after the Sun is so far that its light takes four years to arrive.
topics.keywords: the next star is terribly far the nearest star after the sun is so far that its light takes four years to arrive. if a star you can see tonight vanished this instant, people would keep seeing it for years, and nobody would know.

topics.title: The Sun Is Not Yellow
topics.hook: Every drawing gets it wrong: the Sun is white.
topics.keywords: the sun is not yellow every drawing gets it wrong: the sun is white. never look directly at the sun to check. the damage to your eyes happens without pain and does not heal.

topics.title: Why There Are Two High Tides a Day
topics.hook: The Moon pulls the ocean towards it — so why does the far side bulge too?
topics.keywords: why there are two high tides a day the moon pulls the ocean towards it — so why does the far side bulge too? tides also stretch the solid ground. the land under your feet rises and falls by tens of centimetres twice a day.

topics.title: How Do You Weigh a Planet?
topics.hook: Nobody has ever put a planet on a scale, yet we know what they weigh.
topics.keywords: how do you weigh a planet? nobody has ever put a planet on a scale, yet we know what they weigh. cavendish's result was within about one percent of the modern value, using no electricity and no computer.

topics.title: The Air Is Thinner Than You Think
topics.hook: All the air on Earth is a layer thinner than the skin of an apple.
topics.keywords: the air is thinner than you think all the air on earth is a layer thinner than the skin of an apple. venus has an atmosphere so heavy that standing on its surface would feel like being 900 metres underwater.

topics.title: The Sky on Fire
topics.hook: An aurora is the Sun's weather hitting the Earth's magnetic shield.
topics.keywords: the sky on fire an aurora is the sun's weather hitting the earth's magnetic shield. jupiter and saturn have auroras too, far more powerful than ours, visible in ultraviolet light.

topics.title: The Footprints Are Still There
topics.hook: The bootprints left on the Moon in 1969 have not blurred at all.
topics.keywords: the footprints are still there the bootprints left on the moon in 1969 have not blurred at all. the mirrors left by apollo are still in use — observatories fire lasers at them to measure the moon's distance.

topics.title: You Had More Bones as a Baby
topics.hook: You were born with about 300 bones. You have 206 now.
topics.keywords: you had more bones as a baby you were born with about 300 bones. you have 206 now. the smallest bone in your body sits inside your ear and is about the size of a grain of rice.

topics.title: Your Stomach Rebuilds Itself
topics.hook: Your stomach acid is strong enough to hurt your stomach — so it keeps rebuilding.
topics.keywords: your stomach rebuilds itself your stomach acid is strong enough to hurt your stomach — so it keeps rebuilding. the cells lining your stomach are so exposed that your body replaces them every few days, your whole life.

topics.title: Your Brain Runs on Electricity
topics.hook: Your brain uses about twenty watts — less than a bright light bulb.
topics.keywords: your brain runs on electricity your brain uses about twenty watts — less than a bright light bulb. your brain is about two percent of your weight but uses a fifth of all the energy you burn.

topics.title: Your Blood Vessels Could Circle the Earth
topics.hook: Line up all your blood vessels and they would wrap around the Earth twice.
topics.keywords: your blood vessels could circle the earth line up all your blood vessels and they would wrap around the earth twice. your heart will beat roughly two and a half billion times in an average lifetime, without ever resting.

topics.title: Why You Blink So Much
topics.hook: You blink about fifteen times a minute and hardly ever notice.
topics.keywords: why you blink so much you blink about fifteen times a minute and hardly ever notice. added together, your blinks keep your eyes closed for roughly an hour of every single day.

topics.title: Goosebumps Are Left Over From Fur

topics.keywords: goosebumps are left over from fur goosebumps are your body trying to fluff up fur you no longer have. the muscles that raise your hair are among the few muscles in your body you cannot control on purpose.

topics.title: There Is a Spirit Level in Your Head

topics.keywords: there is a spirit level in your head deep inside each ear are three tiny loops of fluid that tell you which way you are tilting. astronauts feel ill for their first days in space because these organs never stop reporting a fall.

topics.title: How a Cut Stops Bleeding
topics.hook: Your blood has to stay liquid everywhere except exactly where you are bleeding.
topics.keywords: how a cut stops bleeding your blood has to stay liquid everywhere except exactly where you are bleeding. picking a scab restarts the process and usually makes the scar worse — the lid was doing its job.

topics.title: A Fever Is on Your Side
topics.hook: When you have a fever, your body is not broken. It has moved the thermostat on purpose.
topics.keywords: a fever is on your side when you have a fever, your body is not broken. it has moved the thermostat on purpose. cold-blooded animals do a version of this too: an infected lizard will deliberately move to a hotter rock.

topics.title: The Tongue Map Is a Myth
topics.hook: That diagram showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back is simply wrong.
topics.keywords: the tongue map is a myth that diagram showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back is simply wrong. hold your nose and eat a jellybean and you will struggle to name the flavour — until you let go, when it appears instantly.

topics.title: Nobody Else Has Your Fingerprints
topics.hook: Even identical twins, with the same genes, have different fingerprints.
topics.keywords: nobody else has your fingerprints even identical twins, with the same genes, have different fingerprints. koalas have fingerprints so similar to human ones that they can be confused under a microscope.

topics.title: You Are Carrying Trillions of Passengers

topics.keywords: you are carrying trillions of passengers roughly as many bacterial cells live in your body as human cells. antibiotics kill helpful bacteria along with harmful ones, which is why they can upset your stomach for days afterwards.

topics.title: There Is a Hole in Your Vision
topics.hook: Each eye has a blind spot, and your brain hides it from you.
topics.keywords: there is a hole in your vision each eye has a blind spot, and your brain hides it from you. the blind spot in each eye is large enough to hide several full moons in the sky.

topics.title: Why Yawns Are Catching
topics.hook: Reading the word yawn is enough to make some people do it.
topics.keywords: why yawns are catching reading the word yawn is enough to make some people do it. ordinary yawning starts before birth, but catching yawns from other people only begins around age four or five.

topics.title: Why Your Recorded Voice Sounds Wrong
topics.hook: The voice in a recording is the one everyone else has always heard.
topics.keywords: why your recorded voice sounds wrong the voice in a recording is the one everyone else has always heard. some hearing aids use this deliberately, sending sound through the skull bone instead of the ear canal.

topics.title: Forgetting Is a Feature
topics.hook: A brain that remembered everything would work worse, not better.
topics.keywords: forgetting is a feature a brain that remembered everything would work worse, not better. remembering something makes it briefly editable, so a memory recalled often can drift further from the truth than one left alone.

topics.title: You Are Wearing Your Largest Organ
topics.hook: Skin is not a wrapper. It is an organ, and the biggest one you have.
topics.keywords: you are wearing your largest organ skin is not a wrapper. it is an organ, and the biggest one you have. a layer only a fraction of a millimetre thick — the outer dead cells — is what keeps you from drying out.

topics.title: Your Body Runs a Thermostat
topics.hook: You stay at 37°C whether it is freezing outside or blazing hot.
topics.keywords: your body runs a thermostat you stay at 37°c whether it is freezing outside or blazing hot. a person can produce well over a litre of sweat an hour, which is why drinking matters more than resting in the heat.

topics.title: A Runny Nose Is You, Not the Virus
topics.hook: Most of what a cold feels like is your own defence, not the germ.
topics.keywords: a runny nose is you, not the virus most of what a cold feels like is your own defence, not the germ. the average child catches somewhere between six and eight colds a year, which is normal rather than a sign of weakness.

topics.title: Muscles Grow by Being Damaged
topics.hook: Exercise makes you stronger by breaking you slightly, then overbuilding the repair.
topics.keywords: muscles grow by being damaged exercise makes you stronger by breaking you slightly, then overbuilding the repair. the same principle applies to bone: bones exposed to regular load grow denser, which is why astronauts lose bone strength in weightlessness.

topics.title: Why Most People Are Right-Handed
topics.hook: About nine people in ten favour the right hand, and nobody fully knows why.
topics.keywords: why most people are right-handed about nine people in ten favour the right hand, and nobody fully knows why. left-handers are over-represented in sports where an opponent faces you — fencing, boxing, cricket — probably because opponents get less practice against them.

topics.title: Wi-Fi Is Invisible Radio
topics.hook: Wi-Fi is just radio — the same idea as a radio station, but tiny.
topics.keywords: wi-fi is invisible radio wi-fi is just radio — the same idea as a radio station, but tiny. wi-fi waves travel at the speed of light, so the distance across your house costs no time at all.

topics.title: The Internet Runs Under the Ocean

topics.keywords: the internet runs under the ocean almost everything you do online travels through cables on the sea floor. repair ships still fish broken cables up from the sea bed with grappling hooks, much as they did a century ago.

topics.title: A Screen Feels Your Electricity

topics.keywords: a screen feels your electricity your screen does not feel your finger pressing. it feels your body's electricity. a screen like this can tell the difference between ten fingers at once, thousands of times a minute.

topics.title: A Wing Throws Air Downwards

topics.keywords: a wing throws air downwards a plane flies because its wings throw air downwards. a plane can fly upside down — the wing just has to be tilted so it still throws air downwards.

topics.title: A Battery Stores Chemistry, Not Electricity

topics.title: A Fridge Does Not Make Cold

topics.keywords: a fridge does not make cold there is no such thing as cold. a fridge moves heat out, it does not put cold in. an air conditioner is the same machine with the hot end hanging outside the window.

topics.title: Why Planes Leave White Lines

topics.keywords: why planes leave white lines those white trails behind a plane are clouds it made itself. when almost all flights stopped for a few days in 2001, scientists were able to measure how much contrails had been affecting temperatures.

topics.title: The Melted Chocolate Bar

topics.keywords: the melted chocolate bar a microwave oven was invented because a chocolate bar melted in someone's pocket. spencer received about two dollars for the patent, which is what his employer paid for any invention.

topics.title: Your Map Needs Einstein
topics.hook: Satellite navigation would drift ten kilometres off in a day without a correction for time itself.
topics.keywords: your map needs einstein satellite navigation would drift ten kilometres off in a day without a correction for time itself. every time a map app finds you, a theory from 1915 is quietly being used to keep it honest.

topics.title: Why Computers Only Count to One
topics.hook: Everything on a screen is stored as nothing but on and off.
topics.keywords: why computers only count to one everything on a screen is stored as nothing but on and off. a modern phone chip contains more transistors than there are people on earth — by a factor of thousands.

topics.title: Soap Grabs Grease at Both Ends

topics.keywords: soap grabs grease at both ends water alone cannot shift grease. soap acts as a translator between them. soap has been made for over four thousand years, from fat boiled with wood ash, long before anyone knew why it worked.

topics.title: Turning Light Straight Into Electricity
topics.hook: A solar panel has no moving parts at all, yet it makes electricity from sunshine.
topics.keywords: turning light straight into electricity a solar panel has no moving parts at all, yet it makes electricity from sunshine. panels work less well when very hot, which is why a cool bright day can beat a scorching one.

topics.title: How a Speaker Makes Sound

topics.keywords: how a speaker makes sound a speaker is a magnet, a coil of wire, and a piece of card that pushes air. big cones move slowly and make deep notes; small ones move fast and make high notes, which is why speakers come in different sizes.

topics.title: What Is Happening Inside a Lock
topics.hook: A key does not turn a lock. It lines up a row of tiny pins.

topics.title: Nobody Fully Agrees How a Bicycle Balances

topics.keywords: nobody fully agrees how a bicycle balances a moving bicycle can balance itself with nobody on it — and the reason is still argued about. turning a bicycle starts by briefly steering the wrong way — push the right bar to go right. experienced riders do it without knowing.

topics.title: Scientists Can See a Dinosaur's True Colours
topics.hook: For a century, every dinosaur colour in books and films was a total guess. Now some are not.
topics.keywords: scientists can see a dinosaur's true colours for a century, every dinosaur colour in books and films was a total guess. now some are not. the famous armoured dinosaur borealopelta was so well preserved that scientists could tell it had reddish-brown colouring on top and a paler belly, a common camouflage pattern called countershading still used by many animals today to blend into their surroundings from any angle.

topics.title: Nobody Knew What a Dinosaur Was
topics.hook: The first scientifically described dinosaur bone left everyone completely baffled, because the word dinosaur did not exist yet.
topics.keywords: nobody knew what a dinosaur was the first scientifically described dinosaur bone left everyone completely baffled, because the word dinosaur did not exist yet. early reconstructions of iguanodon, made before enough of the skeleton had been found, mistakenly placed a large thumb spike on its nose like a horn — a mistake only corrected decades later when far more complete skeletons were discovered.

topics.title: Older Than Dinosaurs, Older Than Almost Anything
topics.hook: Trilobites crawled the ocean floor for longer than dinosaurs existed — and they were ancient before dinosaurs even began.
topics.keywords: older than dinosaurs, older than almost anything trilobites crawled the ocean floor for longer than dinosaurs existed — and they were ancient before dinosaurs even began. trilobites survived several of earth's mass extinctions before finally going extinct completely around 252 million years ago, in the same catastrophic event that wiped out most other life before dinosaurs ever ruled the planet.

topics.title: How Scientists Know a Fossil's Exact Age
topics.hook: Scientists cannot simply look at a dinosaur bone and know its age. They have to read the rock around it instead.
topics.keywords: how scientists know a fossil's exact age scientists cannot simply look at a dinosaur bone and know its age. they have to read the rock around it instead. the specific radioactive decay rates used in dating rocks have been measured with such extraordinary precision in laboratories that scientists can sometimes date volcanic rock layers to within a margin of just a few thousand years, even for rock that is hundreds of millions of years old.

topics.title: Mammoths Frozen So Well They Still Have Hair
topics.hook: Some woolly mammoths have been found frozen in the Arctic ground so perfectly preserved that their fur, skin and even stomach contents survived.
topics.keywords: mammoths frozen so well they still have hair some woolly mammoths have been found frozen in the arctic ground so perfectly preserved that their fur, skin and even stomach contents survived. climate change melting arctic permafrost is now uncovering new, remarkably preserved mammoth remains more frequently than ever before, even as it threatens the very permafrost conditions that preserved them in the first place.

topics.title: Nothing Was the Hardest Number to Invent
topics.hook: Ancient mathematicians could count enormous armies and measure vast fields, yet the idea of a number for nothing took thousands of years to arrive.
topics.keywords: nothing was the hardest number to invent ancient mathematicians could count enormous armies and measure vast fields, yet the idea of a number for nothing took thousands of years to arrive. without zero acting as a placeholder, writing a number as large as one million would require a completely different, far clumsier system, since zero is precisely what lets 1 and six zeros mean something a thousand times bigger than 1 and three zeros.

topics.title: Why Dividing by Zero Breaks Math
topics.hook: Try dividing any number by zero on a calculator, and instead of an answer, you get an error.
topics.keywords: why dividing by zero breaks math try dividing any number by zero on a calculator, and instead of an answer, you get an error. if you allowed division by zero to simply equal a number like one, you could use ordinary, valid algebra steps to mathematically prove that one equals two — which shows exactly why mathematicians refuse to allow it at all.

topics.title: The Numbers Protecting Your Password
topics.hook: A special kind of number, first studied purely out of curiosity over two thousand years ago, now protects almost everything you do online.
topics.keywords: the numbers protecting your password a special kind of number, first studied purely out of curiosity over two thousand years ago, now protects almost everything you do online. there is no largest prime number — mathematicians have proven, using logic first written down by the ancient greek mathematician euclid, that primes go on forever without ever stopping, no matter how far you count.

topics.title: The Shape Bees Discovered Without Any Maths
topics.hook: A honeycomb is built entirely from six-sided hexagons — the single most efficient shape possible for the job, and bees found it without any classroom.
topics.keywords: the shape bees discovered without any maths a honeycomb is built entirely from six-sided hexagons — the single most efficient shape possible for the job, and bees found it without any classroom. the same efficient hexagon pattern shows up naturally in cooling volcanic rock formations, in dried mud cracking in a hot sun, and in soap bubbles packed tightly together — anywhere nature needs to fill a flat space as efficiently as possible.

topics.title: A Secret Number Pattern Hiding in Plants
topics.hook: Count the petals on many flowers, and you will very often land on the same strange sequence of numbers.
topics.keywords: a secret number pattern hiding in plants count the petals on many flowers, and you will very often land on the same strange sequence of numbers. the ratio between consecutive fibonacci numbers gets closer and closer to a special, famous number called the golden ratio, roughly 1.618, which artists and architects have deliberately used in their own designs for centuries because many people find that particular proportion especially pleasing to look at.

topics.title: Not All Infinities Are Equal
topics.hook: Infinity sounds like the biggest idea possible, one single endless thing. It turns out there are different sizes of infinite.
topics.keywords: not all infinities are equal infinity sounds like the biggest idea possible, one single endless thing. it turns out there are different sizes of infinite. cantor's ideas were so strange and unsettling to other mathematicians at the time that some prominent colleagues attacked him bitterly in public, yet his once-controversial work on different sizes of infinity is now completely accepted and forms a fundamental, essential part of modern mathematics.

topics.title: The Surprise Hiding in a Room of Strangers
topics.hook: Put just 23 random people in one room, and the odds are already better than even that two of them share the exact same birthday.
topics.keywords: the surprise hiding in a room of strangers put just 23 random people in one room, and the odds are already better than even that two of them share the exact same birthday. the exact same underlying mathematics behind the birthday paradox is used by computer scientists to test how easily two completely different pieces of digital data might accidentally produce the same security code, an important consideration in keeping computer systems safe.

topics.title: The King Who Underestimated Doubling
topics.hook: An old legend tells of a king who agreed to a seemingly modest reward, and it nearly bankrupted his entire kingdom.
topics.keywords: the king who underestimated doubling an old legend tells of a king who agreed to a seemingly modest reward, and it nearly bankrupted his entire kingdom. this kind of explosive doubling pattern is called exponential growth, and it is exactly the same underlying mathematics that describes how a single infected person can start an epidemic that grows into millions of cases, or how a tiny starting population of bacteria can multiply into billions within just a single day.

topics.title: The Shape That Repeats Itself Forever
topics.hook: Zoom into certain shapes again and again, and you keep seeing the exact same pattern repeating, no matter how far you zoom.
topics.keywords: the shape that repeats itself forever zoom into certain shapes again and again, and you keep seeing the exact same pattern repeating, no matter how far you zoom. the word fractal was invented in 1975 by the mathematician benoit mandelbrot, who used early computers to generate and explore some of the first fractal images anyone had ever produced, revealing patterns of infinite complexity that no human being had ever actually seen before.

topics.title: Why We Split a Circle Into 360 Pieces
topics.hook: There is no natural law of the universe forcing a circle to be divided into exactly 360 degrees. It is simply a very old habit that stuck.
topics.keywords: why we split a circle into 360 pieces there is no natural law of the universe forcing a circle to be divided into exactly 360 degrees. it is simply a very old habit that stuck. scientists and engineers today also use a completely different, more mathematically natural way of measuring angles called radians, based directly on a circle's own radius rather than an arbitrary historical number, though 360 degrees remains far more familiar and common in everyday, non-scientific life.

topics.title: Counting Before Anyone Had Written Numbers
topics.hook: Long before written number symbols existed, people still needed to count — and they found remarkably clever ways to do it.
topics.keywords: counting before anyone had written numbers long before written number symbols existed, people still needed to count — and they found remarkably clever ways to do it. quipu knots have been found that appear to represent numbers in the thousands with remarkable precision, and researchers are still working today to fully decode some of the more complex surviving examples, since much of the detailed knowledge of exactly how to read them was lost after the spanish conquest of the inca empire.

topics.title: The Number With No End and No Pattern
topics.hook: One special number goes on forever after the decimal point, without ever settling into a repeating pattern.
topics.keywords: the number with no end and no pattern one special number goes on forever after the decimal point, without ever settling into a repeating pattern. some people memorise pi purely for fun and sport, with the current officially recognised world record standing at over 70,000 digits recited entirely from memory, taking the record holder many hours of continuous recitation to complete.

topics.title: Why Your Bathroom Floor Isn't Made of Pentagons
topics.hook: Squares and hexagons can cover a floor perfectly with no gaps. Regular five-sided pentagons simply cannot, no matter how hard you try.
topics.keywords: why your bathroom floor isn't made of pentagons squares and hexagons can cover a floor perfectly with no gaps. regular five-sided pentagons simply cannot, no matter how hard you try. mathematicians eventually discovered special irregular, non-symmetric pentagon shapes — not the perfectly regular kind — that genuinely can tile a floor with no gaps, and new never-before-found tiling pentagon shapes are still occasionally being discovered by dedicated mathematicians even today.

topics.title: Why Counting Jumps by Tens
topics.hook: Almost every counting system used around the world today groups numbers by tens. The reason is attached to your own two hands.
topics.keywords: why counting jumps by tens almost every counting system used around the world today groups numbers by tens. the reason is attached to your own two hands. modern computers do not use base-10 at all internally — they use base-2, called binary, counting using only the digits 0 and 1, because a simple electronic switch only needs to represent two clear, reliable, distinguishable states: fully off or fully on.

topics.title: Bread Is Alive Before You Bake It
topics.hook: A lump of bread dough rises on its own because it is packed with living organisms quietly breathing out gas.
topics.keywords: bread is alive before you bake it a lump of bread dough rises on its own because it is packed with living organisms quietly breathing out gas. sourdough bread uses no separate packaged yeast at all — instead, wild yeast and bacteria naturally floating in the air and already present on the flour itself are deliberately captured and cultivated in a starter, some of which bakeries have kept continuously alive and in active use for well over a hundred years.

topics.title: Chilli Peppers Trick Your Nerves
topics.hook: A spicy chilli does not actually raise your mouth's temperature at all. It simply tricks your nerves into believing it has.
topics.keywords: chilli peppers trick your nerves a spicy chilli does not actually raise your mouth's temperature at all. it simply tricks your nerves into believing it has. scientists measure exactly how spicy a pepper is using something called the scoville scale, and the hottest chilli peppers ever specially bred and measured rate millions of times hotter than an ordinary jalapeño pepper.

topics.title: The Onion's Tiny Chemical Weapon
topics.hook: Slicing into an onion releases an invisible chemical specifically designed by the plant to make you cry.
topics.keywords: the onion's tiny chemical weapon slicing into an onion releases an invisible chemical specifically designed by the plant to make you cry. scientists at a food research institute in new zealand once successfully bred a genetically modified onion specifically engineered to block the enzyme responsible for producing the tear-inducing gas, creating what researchers nicknamed the tearless onion.

topics.title: Food That Is Cooked by Bacteria
topics.hook: Tempeh, yoghurt and tape are not spoiled food. They are food deliberately transformed by carefully chosen, helpful microbes.
topics.keywords: food that is cooked by bacteria tempeh, yoghurt and tape are not spoiled food. they are food deliberately transformed by carefully chosen, helpful microbes. fermentation was one of humanity's very first forms of practical food chemistry, used for thousands of years before anyone anywhere understood that microscopic living organisms were the true, actual cause behind it.

topics.title: The Salt Trick That Freezes Ice Cream
topics.hook: Homemade ice cream recipes call for packing salt directly around ice — not inside the ice cream mixture at all.
topics.keywords: the salt trick that freezes ice cream homemade ice cream recipes call for packing salt directly around ice — not inside the ice cream mixture at all. the exact same basic salt-and-ice principle is why salt is spread on icy roads and pavements during winter in cold countries — it lowers the effective freezing point of the ice enough that it melts even in temperatures that would otherwise keep it frozen solid.

topics.title: Why an Egg Can Never Go Back to Liquid
topics.hook: Once you cook an egg, there is no possible way to turn it back into a raw, runny liquid egg again.
topics.keywords: why an egg can never go back to liquid once you cook an egg, there is no possible way to turn it back into a raw, runny liquid egg again. different proteins inside an egg denature and firm up at slightly different specific temperatures, which is precisely why carefully controlling the exact cooking temperature lets skilled cooks produce a perfectly runny yolk sitting alongside a fully set, firm white in the very same cooked egg.

topics.title: The Tiny Explosion Inside Every Popcorn Kernel
topics.hook: A popcorn kernel is a small, sealed pressure container, and popping it is a genuine tiny explosion.
topics.keywords: the tiny explosion inside every popcorn kernel a popcorn kernel is a small, sealed pressure container, and popping it is a genuine tiny explosion. a popcorn kernel with too little moisture inside it, often because it was stored somewhere too dry for too long, will frequently fail to pop at all, since there simply is not enough trapped steam pressure generated to burst through the tough outer hull.

topics.title: Why a Sliced Apple Turns Brown So Fast
topics.hook: Slice open a fresh apple, and within minutes the cut surface begins turning an unappetising brown.
topics.keywords: why a sliced apple turns brown so fast slice open a fresh apple, and within minutes the cut surface begins turning an unappetising brown. this exact browning reaction, called enzymatic browning, is also precisely responsible for the appealing colour changes seen in tea leaves as they are processed and dried, and in cacao beans as they ferment on their way to eventually becoming chocolate.

topics.title: The Trapped Gas Inside Every Fizzy Bottle
topics.hook: A fizzy drink is ordinary liquid with enormous amounts of invisible gas forcefully dissolved into it, waiting for a chance to escape.
topics.keywords: the trapped gas inside every fizzy bottle a fizzy drink is ordinary liquid with enormous amounts of invisible gas forcefully dissolved into it, waiting for a chance to escape. dropping a few raisins or small mint sweets into a freshly opened fizzy drink gives escaping gas bubbles many extra tiny rough surfaces to cling onto and quickly gather on, which is exactly why the raisins or sweets appear to dance repeatedly up and down through the liquid.

topics.title: The Chemistry Behind Every Golden Crust
topics.hook: Toast, seared meat and roasted coffee all owe their appealing brown colour and rich flavour to the very same chemical reaction.
topics.keywords: the chemistry behind every golden crust toast, seared meat and roasted coffee all owe their appealing brown colour and rich flavour to the very same chemical reaction. caramelisation is a separate but closely related browning reaction that happens when sugar alone is heated intensely with no protein involved at all, which is why plain white sugar melted carefully in a dry pan turns a rich amber-brown and develops a distinctly different flavour from ordinary maillard-browned toast.

topics.title: Why Soaking Makes Vegetables Crisp Again
topics.hook: A wilted, limp vegetable can spring back to crisp life after simply soaking in plain water for a while.
topics.keywords: why soaking makes vegetables crisp again a wilted, limp vegetable can spring back to crisp life after simply soaking in plain water for a while. this same fundamental osmosis principle works powerfully in reverse too — packing vegetables in salt, as happens when making pickles, actively draws water forcefully out of the vegetable cells instead, which is precisely why traditional pickling recipes deliberately produce a distinctly different, notably softer, more tender texture.

topics.title: How Liquid Milk Becomes Solid Cheese
topics.hook: Cheese is essentially milk that has been deliberately, carefully persuaded to fall apart into solid clumps.
topics.keywords: how liquid milk becomes solid cheese cheese is essentially milk that has been deliberately, carefully persuaded to fall apart into solid clumps. some particularly prized, expensive aged cheeses are matured and carefully aged for several years before being sold, during which time naturally occurring enzymes inside the cheese slowly and steadily continue breaking down proteins and fats, which is precisely what produces their intensely concentrated, complex, deeply savoury flavour.

topics.title: Your Eyes Can Change How Food Tastes
topics.hook: Change a food's colour without changing anything else about it at all, and people will often swear the flavour itself has genuinely changed too.
topics.keywords: your eyes can change how food tastes change a food's colour without changing anything else about it at all, and people will often swear the flavour itself has genuinely changed too. in one particularly striking experiment, professional chefs served an entire meal to diners eating in a completely pitch-black room with absolutely no light at all, and many people struggled considerably to correctly identify even very familiar, everyday foods without being able to see them.

topics.title: The Sealed Pot That Cooks in Half the Time
topics.hook: A pressure cooker gets food cooked significantly faster by breaking one of cooking's most basic, familiar rules: water's normal boiling point.
topics.keywords: the sealed pot that cooks in half the time a pressure cooker gets food cooked significantly faster by breaking one of cooking's most basic, familiar rules: water's normal boiling point. this exact relationship also runs precisely in reverse at high altitude: on top of a very tall mountain, where surrounding air pressure is considerably lower than at sea level, water boils at a noticeably lower temperature, which is exactly why cooking instructions and recipe times often specifically need adjusting for people who live at high altitude.
